ratings.reason: A defining instance: one crowdworker retains their role while a Socratic LLM replaces the otherwise-required deliberation partners, directly removing coordination and co-presence. “Crowd without the crowd” is also a notably clear and transferable reframing of asynchronous deliberation.

The title indicates on-demand simulated clients and feedback for counselor practice, matching counterpart substitution and addressing a real scaling constraint. However, the supplied quote describes only the trainer-dependent baseline, so the role mapping and interaction details remain under-evidenced.

AI agents explicitly simulate the co-learners missing from asynchronous education, preserving a collaborative learning configuration for an individual student. The substitution is central and highly portable, though the quote does not show how turns, activities, or visible roles are implemented.

This transposes group motivational interviewing into a one-human, multi-chatbot setting while retaining the social shape of group therapy. Simulating an entire therapeutic group—not merely a single conversational partner—is an unusually strong and interesting expansion of the pattern.

The figure explicitly maps a human-facilitated care procedure onto an asynchronous LLM-facilitated scenario, which strongly resembles counterpart substitution. Yet the language is prospective (“might facilitate”), and the supplied material does not establish an implemented interface or demonstrated outcome, so impact and rebuildability must remain conservative.

Weaver gives one researcher access to synthetic stakeholder conversations that stand in for otherwise unavailable perspectives. The multi-agent stakeholder structure is legible and broadly reusable, although the quote does not fully clarify whether the human occupies one dialog role or mainly observes an agent-only exchange.

An agent can explicitly stand in for an absent family member, removing the need for direct co-presence while preserving interpersonal roles. Mimetic substitution of a specific known person is distinctive, but the evidence does not describe the procedure, interface, or whether the remaining party completes a full interaction alone.

TutorUp cleanly converts tutor–student practice into solo tutor training by having GPT-4o enact students in recognizable engagement-challenge scenarios. The mapping is explicit and rebuildable, though simulated learners for professional practice are now a relatively settled design move.

PairBuddy is the pattern’s canonical pair-programming transplant: the programmer remains while an interactive agent occupies the partner role. The move is exceptionally transferable, and its 2022 timing makes it more design-space-moving than the many later role-play chatbots, although the quote gives limited operational detail.

The agent supplies the opposing partner that peer-argumentation structurally requires, allowing individual practice despite pairing constraints. Maximizing disagreement gives the counterpart a concrete behavioral objective, but the supplied quote stops mid-sentence and describes the access problem more clearly than the implemented loop.

Virtual patients take the absent patient role in clinical-interview practice, with responses conditioned on context and predefined communication criteria. This is a clear, consequential implementation of simulated role-play, but virtual-patient training is a mature and heavily repeated application of the idea.

AI standardized patients directly replace human standardized patients for flexible, on-demand learner practice. The quote strongly confirms the substitution and exposes an important experiential limitation, but it says little about interaction mechanics, and the basic design move is established rather than novel.

The title suggests virtual patients replace peers or supervisors in psychotherapy rehearsal, which would fit the pattern. The supplied quote, however, describes only conventional human role-play and does not show what the virtual patient does, whether the authors specified it, or how the solo loop works.

The quote directly states that peer agents emulate real-time human collaborators for isolated learners, precisely capturing the reduction from multiple humans to one. The approach transfers readily across collaborative learning tasks, but neither its interaction mechanics nor a particularly non-obvious design move is visible here.

Conversate appears to turn a mock interview—interviewee, interviewer, and feedback—into an interactive solo simulation. This is useful and widely transferable, but the evidence quote documents only the human practice-interviewer baseline; the title carries most of the pattern assignment.

Rehearsal directly substitutes simulation for scarce expert conflict role-play, enabling repeated practice of a consequential interpersonal procedure. Conflict resolution is a strong, portable demonstration with plausible outcome impact, though the supplied quote does not reveal the simulated counterpart’s behavior or interface.

“Rehearsal partner” suggests that an LLM occupies the patient or listener role while a clinician practices explanations. But the only evidence is the title, and “co-crafting” may instead describe ordinary AI-assisted authoring rather than preservation of a multi-party medical conversation.

The title’s AI simulations plausibly replace trained actors in high-stakes communication role-play, directly addressing the resource and emotional costs named in the quote. The domain makes the move consequential, but the evidence does not show role mapping or mechanics, and simulated actor practice is not itself novel.

Comparing MIRA’s components with the traditional two-party squiggle game suggests that an AI takes the missing co-player role for solo reflection. That is an intriguing transplant, but the caption provides too little information to confirm the role structure, interaction sequence, or effect.

YES AND explicitly gives an individual the diverse collaborators otherwise required for group ideation, using multiple agents and a named confidence-based turn-taking rule. It is a strong cross-domain example; however, the quote establishes the access problem rather than directly demonstrating the resulting interaction.

Real-time agent substitution for an absent instructor is concrete, consequential, and more dynamic than a fixed chatbot counterpart. It is only a partial match, however: temporary continuity in a possibly multi-trainee session does not necessarily reduce the whole procedure to one human operating alone.

LLM-simulated experts appear to provide the diverse perspectives normally obtained from available human experts during research ideation. The substitution is broadly portable, but simulated expert-persona feedback is increasingly conventional, and the quote describes the availability problem without showing the interaction.

An agentic audio moderator enables a participant to conduct the otherwise moderator-dependent think-aloud procedure without another human, an unusually literal and broadly useful instance of the pattern. The randomized comparison promises consequential evidence, but the supplied quote describes only the human moderator’s role, limiting evidence strength here.

PosterMate constructs the designer’s target audiences as visible agents that provide feedback during design, replacing hard-to-convene reviewers while retaining differentiated audience roles. The mechanism is unusually explicit and readily transferable to many forms of audience-centered critique.

Writer-defined personas provide on-demand substitutes for inaccessible target readers, preserving the writer–audience feedback relationship in a solo workflow. Letting writers define the counterparts adds an important design twist, though the quote itself states only the access problem rather than the feedback mechanics.

The title and quote suggest AI replaces scarce facilitators in medical simulation, but mixed-reality training may still contain multiple human trainees; thus it may remove one role without producing the pattern’s required one-human loop. The provided evidence also does not describe the AI’s facilitation behavior.

A conversational AI supplies the skilled mock interviewer needed for a student to practice technical think-aloud performance alone. This is a clean and useful instance with wide transfer potential, but by 2025 an AI mock interviewer is a highly expected implementation of the pattern.

The title indicates that VR chatbots take the job-interaction partner role for autistic trainees, plausibly enabling solo communication rehearsal. The evidence fragment is truncated before establishing that substitution, and dependence on a specific population and VR setting reduces direct portability.

LLM-based avatars and dynamic role-play plausibly replace human role-play partners in empathy training, addressing the scalability limits identified in the quote. Dynamic avatar role-play is promising, but the available evidence neither identifies the original roles nor confirms a single-user loop.

A human negotiates across the table from an AI, so the system does occupy a role conventionally held by another person. However, the paper’s distinguishing contribution appears to be Bayesian visualization for complex negotiation rather than counterpart simulation; as an exemplar of pat-048, the pattern is supporting infrastructure rather than the central move.
